items.title: Patriarch of Alexandria arrived in Angola for official visit
items.summary: In the early hours of Monday, October 26, 2026, Pope and Patriarch Theodore II of Alexandria and All Africa arrived in Luanda, the capital of Angola, for an official visit to the country in his capacity as Primate of the Patriarchate of Alexandria and spiritual leader of…
items.text:
In the early hours of Monday, October 26, 2026, Pope and Patriarch Theodore II of Alexandria and All Africa arrived in Luanda, the capital of Angola, for an official visit to the country in his capacity as Primate of the Patriarchate of Alexandria and spiritual leader of Orthodoxy on the African continent.

The Patriarch, successor to the Apostle and Evangelist Mark, was received at Luanda Airport with special honours by representatives of the Government of the Republic of Angola; Ms Dina Ehab, Head of the Diplomatic Mission of the Embassy of the Arab Republic of Egypt in Luanda; Mr George Dousopoulos, Honorary Consul of Greece in Angola; and Mr Juliano Ambrósio, Director of External Relations at the Honorary Consulate of Greece.

A highlight of the official visit will be the Patriarch’s scheduled meeting on Tuesday, October 27, with the President of the Republic of Angola, Mr João Lourenço.

It is worth noting that, prior to his election to the Patriarchal Throne of Alexandria, the Patriarch served as Metropolitan of Zimbabwe and Angola, where he carried out extensive missionary and pastoral work. Having gained first-hand knowledge of the needs and distinctive circumstances of these countries, he continues to maintain unbreakable spiritual bonds with their people, whom he came to love and with whom he established personal relationships. They, in turn, have reciprocated his affection with genuine and selfless love.

This visit marks the renewal of these historic and spiritual ties, opening new horizons for strengthening and further developing the Orthodox Church’s missionary presence in Angola, guided by the principles of peaceful coexistence, solidarity and brotherhood, as well as practical service to humanity.

At the same time, the visit highlights the enduring role of the Patriarchate of Alexandria as a bridge of peace, love and cooperation among the peoples of Africa.

The Patriarch is accompanied by two clerics of the Patriarchate of Alexandria: Father Stephanos Muntunemuine, originally from the Congo, who studied at the State University of Rio de Janeiro (UERJ) in Brazil and has an excellent command of Portuguese, the official language of Angola; and Father Paul Nzalambi, originally from Uganda.

Their presence underscores the Patriarch’s vision of identifying, educating, and preparing indigenous African clergy to serve the Orthodox Church in the languages of local communities, while respecting each country’s cultural identity, distinctive circumstances, and particular needs.

items.title_orig: Thessaloniki celebrates Saint Demetrius and 114th Anniversary of Liberation (PHOTOS+VIDEO)
items.text_orig:
Celebrations began in Thessaloniki on Monday morning, October 26, 2026, marking the feast of Saint Demetrius, the city’s patron saint, the 114th anniversary of its liberation, and Greece’s national holiday on October 28.

The festivities commenced with the raising of the Greek flag at the White Tower, accompanied by a 21-gun salute.

At the heart of the celebrations was the Church of Saint Demetrius, where a solemn concelebrated Hierarchical Divine Liturgy was held in the presence of Archbishop Ieronymos of Athens and All Greece.

The Divine Liturgy was presided over by Metropolitan Chrysostomos of Chalkida, Istiaia and the Northern Sporades, with the participation of numerous hierarchs.

Among those concelebrating were Metropolitans Stefanos of Philippi, Chrysostomos of Kyrenia, Chrysostomos of Patras, Georgios of Kitros, David of Grevena, Chrysostomos of Nikopolis and Preveza, Ieronymos of Larissa, Amphilochios of Thera and Dorotheos of Drama.

Bishops Iakovos of Miletoupolis, Nikiforos of Amorion, Bartholomew of Brisbane and Kallinikos of Asterion also participated, alongside Metropolitan Philotheos of Thessaloniki.

Archbishop Ieronymos attended the Divine Liturgy in prayer from the sanctuary.

At 11 a.m. Greece time, the official Doxology began at the Church of Saint Demetrius, presided over by Archbishop Ieronymos in the presence of Greek President Konstantinos Tasoulas.

Representatives of the government, political parties, local authorities, the Armed Forces, security services and other institutions attended the ceremony.

Greek President Tassoulas sends message for freedom, security, peace, progress and prosperity

President of the Hellenic Republic Constantine Tassoulas delivered a message calling for freedom with security, peace, progress and prosperity in a statement made immediately after the official doxology.

“Today, Thessaloniki celebrates a double feast. It celebrates its ever-vigilant guardian, St Dimitrios, and the 114th anniversary of its liberation from approximately five centuries of Ottoman rule,” Tassoulas said.

“We once again reflected in our hearts on the honour we pay to those who fell so that Macedonia and Thessaloniki could become part of the national body. Today, we remembered that 114 years ago, during the First Balkan War, our country, Greece, stood united before the book of its destiny and wrote a new chapter in its history. A chapter that brought the Greek flags and the Greek army back here, to Greek Macedonia.

“Always under the protection of St Dimitrios, Thessaloniki and Macedonia will continue to lead the way and prove worthy of the freedom won at that time. And to be worthy of freedom means enjoying security, peace, progress and prosperity for its people”.

Photos: EUROKINISSI / Tatiana Bolari

items.text_orig:
A mass baptism ceremony was held on Sunday, October 25, 2026, in the village of Khichauri, in Georgia’s Shuakhevi Municipality, within the Diocese of Skhalta.

During the ceremony, approximately 1,500 people were baptized, becoming godchildren of Catholicos-Patriarch Shio III of All Georgia.

items.text:
A solemn Hierarchical Great Vespers service was celebrated at the Church of Saint Demetrius in Thessaloniki on Sunday evening, October 25, 2026, on the eve of the feast of Saint Demetrius the Myrrh-Streamer, the city’s patron saint.

The service was presided over by Metropolitan Chrysostomos of Kyrenia, with numerous Orthodox hierarchs, priests and deacons participating in the celebrations.

Among the concelebrating hierarchs were Metropolitans Chrysostomos of Chalkida, Chrysostomos of Patras, Chrysostomos of Nikopolis and Preveza, Georgios of Kitros, David of Grevena, Stefanos of Philippi, Ieronymos of Larissa, Platon of Langadas, Amphilochios of Thera and Damaskinos of Velestino.

Several bishops also attended, including Iakovos of Miletoupolis, Nikiforos of Amorion, Eirinaios of Rhegion, Christodoulos of Magnesia, Bartholomew of Brisbane, Nifon of Mahajanga and Northern Madagascar, Kallinikos of Asterion and Christodoulos of Neochori.

Metropolitan Philotheos of Thessaloniki also participated in the service, while Metropolitan Chrysostomos of Patras delivered the sermon.

Before the beginning of Vespers, large crowds of faithful filled the Church of Saint Demetrius to honor the memory of the revered martyr and patron saint of Thessaloniki.

items.title: Patriarchate of Alexandria on Jordan Church attack: “Faith transcends all forms of violence”
items.summary: The Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Alexandria and All Africa condemned the terrorist attack on St. George Greek Orthodox Church in Hamoud, Jordan, emphasizing that violence and intolerance violate the fundamental values of peace and human dignity. Patriarch Theodoros II of…
items.text:
The Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Alexandria and All Africa condemned the terrorist attack on St. George Greek Orthodox Church in Hamoud, Jordan, emphasizing that violence and intolerance violate the fundamental values of peace and human dignity.

Patriarch Theodoros II of Alexandria expressed profound sorrow over the loss of innocent lives and extended his condolences to King Abdullah II of Jordan, Patriarch Theophilos III of Jerusalem, the Brotherhood of the Holy Sepulchre, the victims’ families and the Jordanian people.

In its statement, the Patriarchate described the attack on worshippers as a violation of the sanctity of human life and religious freedom, stressing the importance of peaceful coexistence between Christians and Muslims.

It also expressed confidence in the Jordanian authorities to bring those responsible to justice and reaffirmed its solidarity with Jordan, echoing Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s condemnation of the attack.

Patriarch Theodoros offered prayers for the victims and the injured, while conveying his fraternal support to Patriarch Theophilos III and Archbishop Christophoros of Kyriakoupolis, Patriarchal Vicar in Jordan.

“Terrorism has no religion. Love is stronger than hatred, and faith transcends all forms of violence,” the Patriarchate declared.

It concluded by emphasizing that churches and mosques in Jordan and Egypt would continue to serve as symbols of peaceful coexistence and fraternity.

items.title_orig: Patriarch Shio III congratulates Ecumenical Patriarch on 35th Anniversary of Enthronement
items.text_orig:
Catholicos-Patriarch Shio III of All Georgia has sent a congratulatory message to Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew on the 35th anniversary of his enthronement, expressing gratitude for his longstanding support of the Georgian Orthodox Church and the Georgian people.

In his letter, dated October 22, 2026, Patriarch Shio III praised the Ecumenical Patriarch’s ministry, acknowledging the challenges faced by the Church of Constantinople throughout its history and during his 35 years of leadership.

The Georgian Patriarch particularly emphasized Patriarch Bartholomew’s solidarity with Georgia during difficult periods, recalling his message of support during the August 2008 war.

“Your cross today becomes our cross as well,” Patriarch Shio quoted from the Ecumenical Patriarch’s letter, describing those words as an enduring expression of Christian solidarity.

He also expressed gratitude for Patriarch Bartholomew’s close friendship with the late Catholicos-Patriarch Ilia II, recalling his presence at the former Georgian Primate’s funeral and his participation in the nation’s mourning.

Patriarch Shio further thanked the Ecumenical Patriarch for the encouragement and paternal support he had received since the beginning of his own patriarchal ministry.

Referring to Georgia’s recent celebrations marking 1,700 years since the proclamation of Christianity as the state religion, he also expressed appreciation for Patriarch Bartholomew’s congratulatory message on that occasion.

Looking to the future, Patriarch Shio expressed hope that the longstanding spiritual bonds between the Churches of Georgia and Constantinople would continue to strengthen for the benefit of Orthodox unity and peace.

He concluded by wishing Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew good health, longevity and divine assistance in his ministry, praying that he would continue serving the Orthodox Church and promoting love among people.

items.title_orig: Georgian Orthodox Church Delegation meets Ecumenical Patriarch on 35th Anniversary
items.text_orig:
A delegation of the Georgian Orthodox Church has arrived in Constantinople to participate in celebrations marking the 35th anniversary of the enthronement of Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew.

The visit is taking place with the blessing of Catholicos-Patriarch Shio III of All Georgia, Archbishop of Mtskheta-Tbilisi and Metropolitan of Bichvinta and Tskhum-Abkhazia.

The delegation includes Metropolitan Theodore (Chuadze) of Akhaltsikhe and Tao-Klarjeti, Chorepiscopus of the Catholicos-Patriarch; Metropolitan Gerasime (Sharashenidze) of Zugdidi and Tsaishi, Head of the Patriarchate’s Department of Foreign Affairs; and Protopresbyter Giorgi Zviadadze.

During their visit to the Ecumenical Patriarchate, the Georgian representatives met with Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew and conveyed their congratulations on the 35th anniversary of his enthronement.

They also presented a congratulatory letter from Catholicos-Patriarch Shio III, expressing the Georgian Orthodox Church’s good wishes on the occasion.

According to the Georgian Orthodox Church, the meeting took place in a warm and cordial atmosphere.

items.title: Church of Greece: Atmosphere of unity and support for Archbishop of Sinai at Standing Holy Synod (upd)
items.summary: LAST UPDATE: 18:30 An atmosphere of unity and a shared determination to support both Archbishop Symeon of Sinai and St. Catherine’s Monastery on Mount Sinai prevailed during today’s extraordinary meeting of the Standing Holy Synod of the Church of Greece, convened to discuss the…
items.text:
LAST UPDATE: 18:30

An atmosphere of unity and a shared determination to support both Archbishop Symeon of Sinai and St. Catherine’s Monastery on Mount Sinai prevailed during today’s extraordinary meeting of the Standing Holy Synod of the Church of Greece, convened to discuss the issue.

According to information obtained by orthodoxtimes.com, the meeting was marked by a spirit of unity, with unanimous support expressed for the monastery and genuine concern over its future legal status following the expected publication of the ruling by Egypt’s Supreme Court of Cassation on October 24.

According to the same sources, the Synodal Metropolitans were briefed by Archbishop Ieronymos of Athens and All Greece, who presided over the meeting, on the latest judicial developments and the current situation at the monastery.

All the hierarchs expressed their support for Archbishop Symeon of Sinai, with whom they also held a brief online meeting. During their conversation, they assured him of the Church of Greece’s support regarding the challenges facing St. Catherine’s Monastery and listened to his views on the matter.

Subsequently, the Secretary General for Religious Affairs, Giorgos Kalantzis, was invited to participate in the meeting, where he remained for approximately one hour.

According to information obtained by orthodoxtimes.gr , Secretary Kalantzis provided the Synodal Metropolitans with clarifications considered necessary to give the Standing Holy Synod a comprehensive understanding of the efforts being undertaken by the Greek government to secure the best possible outcome for the monastery’s future.

Furthermore, the Standing Holy Synod decided to send a letter to Archbishop Symeon expressing its support for efforts to reach a mutually beneficial agreement with the Egyptian state.

Sources speaking to orthodoxtimes.com described the atmosphere as positive, particularly regarding bilateral relations between Greece and Egypt, while also expressing optimism about the final ruling of the Egyptian judicial authorities.

Following the conclusion of the meeting, the Synodal Metropolitans departed without making any statements, and no official briefing or announcement was issued by the Synod.

Although the Church of Greece has no institutional or administrative jurisdiction over the affairs of St. Catherine’s Monastery, the extraordinary meeting was convened to brief the Synodal Metropolitans and demonstrate support for the monastic brotherhood and Archbishop Symeon of Sinai.

According to information available to orthodoxtimes.com , the position adopted by the monastery’s brotherhood is also considered crucial, as reports so far suggest that some monks do not appear to fully appreciate the seriousness of the situation concerning the monastery’s future.

It is also particularly significant that three major Orthodox Churches, the Ecumenical Patriarchate, the Patriarchate of Jerusalem, and the Church of Greece, have expressed their unwavering support for all members of the monastic brotherhood and Archbishop Symeon of Sinai.

By Efi Efthymiou

Translated by: Konstantinos Menyktas

items.title_orig: Archbishop Georgios calls for new Approach to Cyprus Issue, defends dialogue with the Vatican
items.text_orig:
Archbishop Georgios of Cyprus has called for a change in the strategy pursued to safeguard the rights of the Republic of Cyprus, expressing concern that current developments in the Cyprus issue are not leading to meaningful progress.

Speaking to the Cyprus Broadcasting Corporation (RIK), the Archbishop also defended dialogue with the Roman Catholic Church, rejected accusations of concelebration with Catholic clergy, and addressed the controversy surrounding the Monastery of Saint Avvakoum.

Archbishop Calls for Change in Cyprus Strategy

Referring to the Cyprus issue, Archbishop Georgios argued that the concessions made so far have failed to produce tangible results.

He expressed reservations about the emphasis placed on opening new crossing points between the government-controlled and Turkish-occupied areas of Cyprus, stressing that such measures should not be confused with a comprehensive settlement.

According to the Archbishop, the current situation risks consolidating the existing realities on the ground rather than bringing the island closer to reunification.

He called on Greeks in Cyprus, Greece and the diaspora to coordinate their efforts, strengthen international alliances and make greater use of available diplomatic and political means.

Archbishop Georgios emphasized that the Cyprus issue remains a question of invasion, occupation and human rights violations. He also argued that Cyprus and Greece, as European Union member states, should make full use of the opportunities provided by their EU membership.

“Whatever other Europeans enjoy, we should enjoy as well,” he stated.

Restoration of Churches in Occupied Cyprus

The Archbishop also raised concerns about the restoration of churches and religious monuments in the occupied areas of Cyprus.

He noted that although restoration projects receive financial support from the Greek Cypriot side and the European Union, the buildings are not necessarily returned to their original religious use.

According to Archbishop Georgios, some restored churches continue to serve other purposes, despite the completion of conservation work.

He explained that the Church supports restoration efforts to prevent the deterioration or collapse of historic religious monuments and preserve them for future generations. However, he stressed that the ultimate objective should also include restoring their original function as places of Christian worship.

Defending Dialogue with the Roman Catholic Church

Addressing criticism of the Church of Cyprus’s contacts with the Roman Catholic Church, Archbishop Georgios defended theological dialogue as an essential means of exploring the shared Christian tradition of the first millennium, when Eastern and Western Christianity were united.

“We made no concessions. We did not engage in any concelebration,” he stated, firmly rejecting accusations that Orthodox ecclesiastical principles had been compromised.

The Archbishop also criticized manifestations of religious fanaticism, warning that such attitudes are directed not only against Christians of other denominations but also against fellow Orthodox believers.

He emphasized that Christians should seek ways to cooperate in addressing contemporary challenges without abandoning their doctrinal convictions.

Responding to questions about disagreements within the Holy Synod of the Church of Cyprus, he questioned how the search for truth could take place without dialogue.

Vatican Diplomacy and Christians in the Middle East

Archbishop Georgios also highlighted the importance of maintaining relations with the Holy See, particularly regarding international support for Cyprus.

“We also seek the support of the Holy See on our national issue, as it has many ambassadors, nuncios, accredited throughout the world,” he said.

He explained that the Vatican’s extensive diplomatic network could help bring greater international attention to the Cyprus issue.

The Archbishop also expressed concern about the situation facing Christian communities in the Middle East.

He stressed that religious leaders have a responsibility to cooperate with political authorities to create conditions that allow Christians to remain in their ancestral homelands rather than being forced to leave.

Archbishop Addresses Saint Avvakoum Monastery Controversy

Turning to the controversy surrounding the Monastery of Saint Avvakoum, Archbishop Georgios reiterated the Church’s position on the consequences of the deposition of clergy.

He explained that, under Orthodox canonical discipline, clergy who have been formally defrocked are no longer authorized to perform valid sacramental or sanctifying acts.

The Archbishop urged the faithful not to be misled by individuals who have been removed from the priesthood and emphasized the importance of understanding and respecting ecclesiastical decisions.

Source: Sigmalive , translated by: Konstantinos Menyktas

items.title_orig: The Territory of Creativity
items.text_orig:
The Nativity of Christ by Olga Shalamova, 2025. Aged wood, egg tempera. In this work, I was fascinated to watch the image literally emerge from the dark surface of the panel. In icon painting, we very, very often paint both faces and garments from dark to light, as though drawing the image out of nonexistence. Here, the dark wood of the old panel literally became the mysterious atmosphere of Christmas night. What I like about working in this way is that you are not thinking about formal approaches in icon painting; you are thinking about the image itself, about the composition as a whole.

This article was originally published in the magazine “Slovo i Kamen” (“Word and Stone”) .

Icon Painter and Artist

From book to book, from trip to trip, from one person to the next, encounters keep happening – and each time something important comes into view. For me, one of the most meaningful was meeting Todor Mitrovic. It was in the fall of 2010, when St. Petersburg hosted an icon-painting symposium organized by Georgios Kordis. Artists came from Romania, Serbia, and Bulgaria; and there were Russians too: Philip Davydov and myself, along with Zhenya Davydenko and Yaroslavа Alekseeva. The artists were invited for three days, during which they worked on monumental compositions. The event was open to the public—people could drop in and watch the process. But the best part was talking with one another, and that turned out to be priceless.

What struck me in Todor’s work was the realization that a contemporary icon does not have to be a frozen mannequin, some kind of “proper” mask—it can be deeply sincere, naive, and joyful. These were not copies or stylizations; they were icons, but different from any I had seen before. What won me over most was that he was a true artist. The very term “icon painter” often imposes limitations, cutting off the creative process, but here I saw an icon painter and an artist in the fullest sense.

The atmosphere of the symposium was extraordinary as well, and we have all remained friends ever since. Later, I interviewed Todor for the almanac Gifts. He spoke fascinatingly about the nature of the canon, referring to the Apostle Paul: originally, “canon” was understood as a measure of piety, and only over time did it acquire external boundaries and rules.

For all my affection for Todor’s work, I try not to get carried away with borrowing particular formal approaches. What I did take from him was a sense of freedom in working with the icon—a freedom grounded in tradition and in the understanding that tradition has always been fluid and has always reflected its time. For me, icon painting is a high art—one that you cannot truly enter unless you are an artist.

The Philosophy of the Creative Process and the “Miracle” of Making Art

The eternal question for any artist is how not to become rigid in the approaches one has discovered and, perhaps without even noticing it, begin to repeat oneself. Why does one artist stop searching and start reproducing their own solutions, while another continues to create something new throughout their life and remains curious about the world?

I think what matters most here is that moment of genuine wonder—the ability to see something new, to learn, to make mistakes, even when you are eighty or ninety years old. What matters is a sense of the creative process as something alive, along with an awareness of your own imperfection. And perhaps it is also important, like the ancient Chinese painters, to switch the brush from your right hand to your left when you feel yourself beginning to work mechanically.

Creativity as Daily Routine

For me, creativity is first and foremost daily work. Inspiration never simply appears on its own. First, you have to enter the process, the routine itself. You simply come into the studio and begin to work, and gradually you enter a kind of state of flow in which everything becomes logical and clear. This state does not descend upon you—you have to enter it yourself. But at the same time, this does not mean that everything comes in a single breath or that you never make mistakes.

The Annunciation to the Mother of God by Olga Shalamova, 2025. Handmade mulberry paper, mixed media.

Panels and tiles are substantial, heavy supports that require both special preparation and proper storage. So discovering handmade mulberry paper as a surface to work on was a real find for me. It is thin and uneven, with areas where the layer becomes thinner and even small bare patches. There are all kinds of hard inclusions and irregularities, and I find the character of this surface fascinating. Whatever material I work with, I greatly value its individual character. I don’t want to neutralize or correct it; on the contrary, I want to feel it and bring it out, because the surface itself can already determine the expressive quality of the image. Here, I particularly enjoyed working with a dry, coarse brush and seeing the uneven, lively brushstroke it produces. I make works like this without a preliminary drawing, working boldly and freely from the very beginning. There is almost no possibility of making corrections, and I like that very much, because I think the energy with which the work is made is transmitted to the viewer. The surface of the paper itself does not allow you to become absorbed in detail, and in this way the material itself leaves the viewer space for co-creation.

For a while, those mistakes in my work—when I reached a dead end and did not know what to do next, when I redid something several times and the work still refused to come together—upset me deeply, and I experienced such moments very intensely, until I realized that this is the very essence of my work: these dead ends are always fascinating, and they are always points of growth.

I can’t say that I deliberately wait for such moments, but when everything falls apart—the composition collapses, the color doesn’t work the way I intended, or some other problem arises—I see it as the best moment in the process, and I have come to love this state.

This is precisely when you become fully engaged, mobilizing all your knowledge, experience, and strength. You look at the failure and think: interesting—how do I find my way out of this maze? You are already inside the process, but standing among the ruins, and how it all comes together depends entirely on you. And to me, this says something very important about the work of an icon painter.

As long as we are making mistakes, searching, and reworking things, there is definitely something real in our work—something we have had to struggle for, even if only a little.

There are countless videos online in which an icon painter appears as an inspired creator who walks up to a wall or a panel and immediately produces a masterpiece. This is certainly beautiful, but it is only a screen concealing the real, difficult work—the work in which you stumble, doubt yourself, redo things, and keep going. And that is normal. It is part of the process.

On Canon, Tradition, and Boundaries in Church Art

For an icon painter, reflecting on canon and on the limits of what is permissible in church art is an ongoing process. I was once asked how acceptable it is to place very avant-garde icons—such as those of the Lviv school—in an Orthodox church. They seem to be icons, and yet somehow they seem strange. So what do we do with that?

I do have an answer to this question, but I can only offer my own perspective, based on a kind of ideal situation. Let us imagine an ideal world: the parishioners of a particular church commission icons from Lviv artists because they themselves are able to decide what kind of space they want to pray in. And they want to pray surrounded by precisely these images because, for these particular people, this art is liturgical; it is in images like these that they see Christ most clearly. In that case, who are we to forbid them?

To question whether particular icons have a legitimate place in a church seems to me somewhat presumptuous. We want to reduce all church art to a handful of rules. For some reason, we find it difficult to accept, deep down, that we are all very, very different. For one person, an icon has to be dark and old, set in a gilded frame; for another, it is a reinterpretation of Old Russian icons; for someone else, it is the imagery of Jerzy Nowosielski. We are all different, and we can attend different churches where, perhaps one day, the visual language will differ as well. And it seems to me that the fact that we are all so different is a tremendous gift.

This urge to regulate everything is a huge problem of our time—and, in particular, of the discourse surrounding the icon.

For me, this desire to make everything uniform and to define what an icon should be carries clear echoes of the Soviet era. I believe that it is the community, and the community alone, that can and should decide. And if, out of a great many Gospels, not one, not two, but four were chosen, that is a good example for us of how to be more tolerant in our judgments about what is permissible in an icon and what is not.

It is wonderful when a community has its own icon painter. Suppose that in my community, besides me, there is another artist who paints icons for my church—I would be very happy about that. Even if his approach were not particularly close to my own, it would still be deeply satisfying, on a human level, to know that this work was born within the community, that I know this icon painter and everyone around me knows him as well.

Perhaps these icons would not be perfect and would not meet certain so-called “high standards,” but if they are accepted by the community, why should someone come in and say, “Look, these are bad icons—or bad murals—tear them down at once”?

When we talk about the path of young icon painters and their search for a visual language of their own, I don’t think that everyone necessarily has to be “creative.”

The Resurrection of Christ by Olga Shalamova, 2024. Old ceiling panel, egg tempera. In every work, it is important for me to think about how the meaning of the image is revealed through composition, color, and details. Here, everything is built on the juxtaposition of two geometric forms—the oval and the rectangle: the rounded mandorla, in whose radiance Christ is depicted, and the rectangle of hell. On the one hand, it is a very simple visual idea, but it is precisely this simplicity that leaves space for reflection. Instead of the familiar title “The Descent into Hell,” I wanted the icon to proclaim the Victory of Life. The phrase “Christ is risen, and life reigns” comes from the Paschal Homily of St. John Chrysostom, which is read in churches on the night of Pascha. The words of the Apostle Paul are heard there as well: “O death, where is your sting? O hell, where is your victory?” (1 Cor. 15:55). Such an inscription does not simply accompany the image—it expands its field of meaning and makes the inner dialogue with the image deeper and more personal.

We are born with certain gifts. We are all very, very different, and I think our task is not to invent something new, but to discover within ourselves what has already been given to us.

If you make beautiful copies, then perhaps that is your gift. And that, too, can be a genuine form of service. Above all, it is important to learn to listen to yourself and truly hear yourself. Because only through this inner honesty is a genuine conversation with God possible.

There is a great deal of emphasis on obedience in church life, and it is indeed important. But no priest can look inside your soul and determine your calling for you. For me, this is precisely what Christianity is about: personal responsibility before God and inner freedom.

items.title_orig: Archbishop Georgios of Cyprus to meet Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican in October
items.text_orig:
Archbishop Georgios of Cyprus is expected to visit the Vatican from October 19 to 21, 2026, where he will hold meetings with Pope Leo XIV and other senior officials of the Roman Catholic Church.

The discussions are expected to focus on ecclesiastical matters, relations between the Orthodox and Roman Catholic Churches, and the possibility of bringing the Holy Relic of the Head of Apostle Paul to Cyprus.

One of the central issues on the agenda will be the proposed transfer of the sacred relic, an initiative of particular religious significance for the Church of Cyprus.

The visit will also provide an opportunity to strengthen dialogue between the two Churches and discuss matters of mutual interest.

The Vatican maintains religious ties with Cyprus, which is home to Roman Catholic communities, including Latin Catholics and Maronites.

Archbishop Georgios’s upcoming meetings are expected to address both bilateral ecclesiastical relations and the arrangements surrounding the proposed transfer of the relic.

Source: simgalive.com

items.title_orig: Feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross celebrated in Warsaw
items.text_orig:
The Orthodox Church commemorated the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, a feast recalling the discovery of the Cross of Christ in Jerusalem and its veneration by the faithful.

According to Church tradition, Saint Helena, mother of Emperor Constantine the Great, traveled to Jerusalem in search of the places associated with the final events of Christ’s earthly life. Tradition holds that three crosses were discovered beneath the ruins of a pagan temple, with the True Cross identified after contact with it restored a deceased person to life.

The discovery is believed to have taken place around 325 or 326. Emperor Constantine subsequently began constructing churches in Jerusalem, including the Basilica of the Resurrection near Golgotha and the Holy Sepulchre, which was consecrated around 335.

The veneration of the Cross gradually developed into a separate feast known as the Exaltation of the Holy Cross. Because of its connection with Christ’s Passion and death, the day is observed as a fast in the Orthodox Church.

One of the feast’s distinctive liturgical elements is the solemn elevation of the Cross during Matins. The bishop raises and lowers the Cross while blessing the four points of the compass, as the choir repeatedly chants “Lord, have mercy.” Afterwards, the Cross is placed in the center of the church for veneration by the faithful.

At the Cathedral of Saint Mary Magdalene in Warsaw, the All-Night Vigil and the rite of the elevation of the Holy Cross were presided over by Bishop Paweł of Hajnówka.

Metropolitan Sawa prayed in the sanctuary during the service.

Photos: Protodeacon I. Kutovyi

items.title_orig: A Vision for Orthodoxy in Puerto Rico
items.text_orig:
Completed Design for Misión Ortodoxa San Juan Clímaco (ROCOR) in San Germán, Puerto Rico. Designed by Andrew Gould/New World Byzantine.

In 2023, I was asked to consult on the design for the first Russian-Orthodox church in Puerto Rico. In the three years since, this has turned into one of the most interesting projects of my career. I believe it may also prove to be one of the most important. It will set the style for Orthodoxy in Puerto Rico – a cultural fusion that has never before been given much consideration. And I hope that it will do so with such compelling success that it will serve as a guide and inspiration for Orthodox design all across Latin America.

Misión Ortodoxa San Juan Clímaco (ROCOR) was founded in 2009 by Fr. Gregorio Justiniano. Fr. Gregorio, a Puerto Rican convert to Orthodoxy from Pentecostalism, learned of the ancient faith while living in the United States. In time, he and his family became deeply dedicated to the service of Christ’s Church, with two of his sons entering the priesthood as monks. Fr. Gregory was ordained a priest in 2006. Three years later, with the blessing of Metropolitan Nicholas of the Carpathian-Russian Diocese and Metropolitan Hilarion, First Hierarch of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia, Father Gregorio and his wife sold their home in Danbury, Connecticut, and returned to their roots in San Germán, Puerto Rico. There they restored an old house on a beautiful estate, and established a house chapel from which to serve the mission.

The mission property in San Germán. The current chapel is in the house to the left, and the new church is to go on the hilltop to the right.

In 2020, as the community grew to fill the chapel, Fr Gregorio set aside land near his house on which to build their church. Unsure how the church should look, he decided to take as a model the cemetery chapel of Jordanville Monastery, which follows the architectural form of old churches in Pskov. Fr Gregorio visited and measured the chapel, and hired a Puerto Rican engineering firm to adapt the design and draw up plans for the church. In time, however, the community grew uncertain if the design was right for them, as it looked only Russian, and seemed not to reflect their Puerto Rican heritage. In 2023, following the advice of his son, master iconographer Fr. Silouan Justiniano, Fr. Gregorio asked me to review the design.

I agreed that the proposed design seemed not to fit with Puerto Rican culture in any way. I suggested that a new design, keeping with the simple Russian form they liked, but styled and ornamented in the manner of historic Puerto-Rican architecture, would better serve their community. It would allow them to feel that they offer their prayers not as converts to Russian culture, but as Puerto Ricans who retain their culture and identity within the Orthodox Faith.

I travelled to Puerto Rico that November to view the site, study the local architecture, meet with the engineering team, and to share Thanksgiving dinner with Fr. Gregorio’s family. That week was one of great joy and creative inspiration to me. I began by spending two days in old San Juan, the historic capital. It’s an amazing and exquisitely preserved city of old Spanish-Baroque buildings painted in a blaze of cheerful colors. San Juan contains many great churches. Some are so old that their architecture is in the medieval Gothic style, and others feature domes, barrel vaults, and frescoes, not unlike Orthodox churches. With such amazing cultural heritage, I thought, how could we build a new church that does not live up to this treasury of beauty?

Buildings I photographed in Old San Juan.

A beautiful red-and-white house in Old San Juan serves as inspiration for the church’s color scheme.

Church of San José in Old San Juan. Construction on this church started in 1528.

Fr. Gregorio took me on drive across Puerto Rico, visiting several towns. Everywhere, I observed the same thing. The old buildings were colorful, thoughtfully designed, covered in cheerful stucco ornamentation, and exuded a joyful, charming beauty. But the newer buildings were invariably plain, utilitarian, and haphazard. Most of them were painted boring colors and poorly maintained, as if making the best of them were not even worth the trouble. My observations suggested that a considerable loss of cultural and artistic confidence afflicts modern Puerto Rico, at least with regards to architecture.

I suggested something bold, but necessary, to Fr. Gregorio: Why do we not build your church like the old buildings? Not just generally beautiful, but specifically like these old Puerto Rican buildings – solid masonry walls, beamed ceilings, tiled floors, covered in Spanish-Baroque stucco ornament, and painted a brilliant bright color. Fr. Gregorio responded that no one has built like that in Puerto Rico for a very long time. But why not? Perhaps the Orthodox Church should be the first to try it.

Standing on the site of the future church with Frs. Gregorio and Silouan.

I’ve rarely been so excited to put pencil to paper. I could see that the Puerto-Rican style was all about materials, ornament, and colors. These characteristics could be applied to any building form. So, I took the traditional Russian form that the community liked – a cube-shaped nave with a hipped-roof and onion-dome, and rooms to the east and west for altar and narthex. How, I asked myself, would Puerto Rican builders of the old days render this form? With a big overhanging roof with exposed rafter tails to shed the tropical rain, I figured. Wrought-iron canopies to protect the doors. Classical pilasters to define the corners and frame the doorways. Curvy baroque parapets to terminate the gables. A high-contrast red-and-white paint scheme to emphasize the ornamentation. On the interior, thick plastered walls and a tile floor to keep cool. Ceilings and lintels built from rustic wooden beams.

My first concept sketch for the church, done on site.

The fully-developed exterior design, from 2025.

I knew the iconostasis would be absolutely key to the project. These small Russian churches with cube-shaped naves invariably have an iconostasis that covers the entire east wall. Since there are no columns or other complications to the architecture, the iconostasis is the only complexity to the space, and completely defines its character.

Remarkably, the perfect inspiration for the iconostasis was to be found just down the road, in the local town center. The town of San Germán is the second oldest in Puerto Rico, and was the island’s western capital in the sixteenth century. At one end of San Germán’s central avenue there stands a beautiful church remaining from a monastery established in 1609 – El Convento de Santo Domingo de Porta Coeli. The church is now Puerto Rico’s national museum of religious art, and contains an important collection of baroque paintings and sculptures. The church’s retablo (altarpiece) dates from the 18 th -century, and is likely the only surviving Puerto-Rican-made altarpiece. It’s a marvelous construction, elegantly designed, but with a folkish vernacular flair. It has great presence and character.

Visiting El Convento de Santo Domingo de Porta Coeli in San Germán with Fr. Silouan Justiniano.

The eighteenth-century altarpiece at El Convento Porta Coeli.

A detail of the carved-wood altarpiece.

Frs. Gregorio and Silouan admiring the old houses of San Germán.

When I saw the altarpiece in San Germán, I immediately felt that this must be our model for the iconostasis. Like most Spanish retablos , it’s structured with twisting “Solomonic” columns framing statues of saints. I could easily picture it with painted icons substituted for the statues – its overall design would be almost identical to a Russian Baroque iconostasis, but the vernacular style of the carving would retain its identity as Puerto Rican.

After returning to my office in Charleston, construction at Holy Cross Monastery and elsewhere consumed all my attention, and it was about a year before I had time to return to the project. Finally, in 2025, I worked out a detailed and buildable design for the church, working with the formed-concrete construction system widely used in Puerto Rico. The local engineers redid their structural, mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and civil drawings to conform to my new church design, and the project was submitted to the lengthy government permitting process.

In the meantime, much design work remained to do on the decorative parts – the stucco ornamentation, the wrought-iron work, and the iconostasis. Designing good ornamentation can easily take more time than designing an entire building. Fortuitously, I was able to hire a new assistant, Jakob Janssen, in 2025. Jakob was trained at Notre Dame’s excellent master’s program in classical architecture. He did much of the time-consuming design work, doing detailed research on Spanish-baroque ornament, drafting all the elaborate pilasters, pediments, and scroll-work in AutoCAD, and producing large-scale template drawings for the masons to work from. Ultimately, Jakob painted a beautiful watercolor rendering of the church situated on its hilltop site.

Jakob’s perspective drawing of the church on its hilltop site.

The completed watercolor rendering.

For the iconostasis, Jakob and I looked at hundreds of images of Spanish retablos and Russian-Baroque iconostases, studying their similarities and differences. We developed numerous iterations of our iconostasis design, considering how they would feel in the space, and how well they would support the iconography. Ultimately, we settled on a design that is completely true to the style of woodwork expressed in the San Germán retablo , while also functioning completely within the tradition of an Orthodox iconostasis.

The interior rendering was particularly challenging. Fr. Silouan Justiniano plans to paint the icons, and asked us to render them with green backgrounds and gold haloes. The play of light, colors, and reflections, off the plaster, varnished wood, and shiny metal would be quite complex. To create a realistic image, we used a hybrid technique, combining pencil-drafted outlines, watercolor-painted icons, and computer-rendered light and shadow.

Jakob’s pencil rendering of the church interior with our iconostasis design.

The completed interior rendering.

One small element remained to be designed. Hieromonk Daniel, second priest of the mission, and their media specialist, asked us if we might design a graphical logo for the parish – one that would complement the church design. We decided to use the form of baroque cartouche, framing within it a 3-bar Russian cross, and a heraldic ladder for their dedication to St. John Climacus. For the final version of the logo, we got out ink and quill pens, and hand-drew it the way it would have been done in the eighteenth century, aiming for how a cartouche might look on an old Spanish royal document or map.

Drawing the cartouche logo with ink and quill.

The completed logo.

I particularly enjoyed this small part of the commission, as it seemed like placing a literal seal on the project – and to summarize the whole concept behind it in a single gesture – a logo for the right-glory of the Logos.

Misión Ortodoxa San Juan Clímaco now has a new website featuring the church design and logo, and has begun their public fundraising campaign. Please consider supporting this important project! The construction of such a church will be a light for Orthodoxy in Latin America. And it will provide a much-needed opportunity for Puerto Rican builders and craftsmen to practice artisanal trades that have been nearly lost from the island’s culture.

items.title_orig: Metropolitan Sawa celebrates Nativity of the Theotokos at Hagia Sophia Church in Warsaw
items.text_orig:
Metropolitan Sawa of Warsaw and All Poland presided over the Divine Liturgy for the feast of the Nativity of the Theotokos at the Hagia Sophia Church in Warsaw.

The celebration began on the eve of the feast with an All-Night Vigil. On the feast day, the blessing of water was followed by the Divine Liturgy, celebrated by Metropolitan Sawa together with Bishop Warsonofiusz of Siemiatycze and attending clergy.

In his homily, Bishop Warsonofiusz reflected on Divine Wisdom and the harmony of creation, stressing that humanity was created to live in communion with God, the world and one another, but that this relationship was disrupted by sin.

He also emphasized the central place of the Theotokos in the mystery of the Incarnation, noting that her maternal closeness to the faithful is connected with her own experience of love and suffering.

Bishop Warsonofiusz encouraged the faithful to turn frequently to the Virgin Mary, not only with their everyday concerns and prayers for loved ones, but also with confidence that she remains close to those in need.

At the conclusion of the service, Metropolitan Sawa highlighted the significance of the Nativity of the Theotokos in God’s plan of salvation.

He stressed that by receiving the Son of God in her womb, the Virgin Mary became the Mother of God the Word, while Christ’s assumption of human nature opened the way for humanity to restore its communion with the Creator.

Metropolitan Sawa also recalled the history of the Hagia Sophia churches in Białystok and Warsaw, saying that their construction was inspired by his visit to Hagia Sophia in Constantinople.

He thanked all those who support parish life in Warsaw’s Ursynów district, with particular reference to the parish choir of Saint Romanos the Melodist.

The celebrations concluded with a communal meal.

Text: Fr Adam Magruk, Photos: Fr Paweł Korobeinikov, Deacon Andrzej Golimont

items.title_orig: Metropolitan Sawa: Saint Job of Pochaev remains a model of faith and devotion
items.text_orig:
The Orthodox Church in Poland commemorated Saint Job, Abbot of Pochaev, on September 10, with celebrations at the Church of Saint Nicholas the Wonderworker in Kośna.

The Divine Liturgy was presided over by Archbishop Grzegorz of Bielsk, together with Bishop Paweł of Hajnówka and Bishop Warsonofiusz of Siemiatycze, accompanied by clergy of the Warsaw-Bielsk Diocese. Metropolitan Sawa of Warsaw and All Poland attended the service in prayer.

In his address, Metropolitan Sawa highlighted the importance of heavenly patrons in the life of Orthodox Christians, describing Saint Job as an example of complete dedication to God and a defender of the Orthodox faith and tradition.

The Metropolitan stressed that Saint Job’s example remains relevant both for clergy and the faithful, particularly in challenging times.

“The times in which we live are difficult and complex, but with Christ we are strong,” Metropolitan Sawa said.

He also emphasized that unity and harmony require obedience to God, patience and a willingness to follow His will.

Concluding his address, Metropolitan Sawa thanked the clergy and faithful for their common prayer and invoked God’s blessing upon all those present.

items.title_orig: Every Style of Georgian Chant Explained with Dr. John Graham
items.text_orig:
Why does the same ancient chant melody sound completely different depending on which corner of Georgia you’re standing in?

Musicologist John A. Graham returns for Part 2 of our exploration of Georgian Orthodox chant, this time going deep into the three great transcribed monastery schools: Gelati, Shemokmedi, and Svetitskhoveli. At the heart of Graham’s research is a fascinating argument: the schools inherited essentially the same model melodies, but each region learned to harmonize and ornament them through the sound-world of its own Georgian folk polyphony. The chanters who sang in church were often the same master singers who performed at the feast table afterward, and the two traditions shaped one another over generations.

We explore the east–west divide created by the Likhi Range, the nearly lost chant tradition of Svaneti, whether Georgian congregations historically sang, the ninth chords of Gurian polyphony, voice crossing, the three levels of ornamentation, the ornamented middle voice of Vasil Karbelashvili, the musical ‘signatures’ that let scholars identify individual chanters in manuscripts, and the controversy over whether Trio Mandili represents authentic Georgian folklore.

items.title_orig: Greek Ambassador to Poland receives Church honor during farewell visit to Metropolitan Sawa
items.text_orig:
On Monday, August 24, 2026, Metropolitan Sawa of Warsaw and All Poland received Niki Kamba, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Hellenic Republic to Poland, for a farewell meeting.

The Greek Ambassador visited the Metropolitan as she prepares to conclude her diplomatic tenure in Poland. During the meeting, she expressed her gratitude to Metropolitan Sawa for their cooperation and the good relations maintained throughout her term.

In recognition of her contribution and as a token of appreciation, Metropolitan Sawa awarded Ambassador Kamba the Order of Saint Mary Magdalene.

The meeting marked the conclusion of a period of cooperation between the Greek diplomatic mission in Poland and the Polish Autocephalous Orthodox Church.

items.title_orig: Transfiguration celebrated at St Demetrius Monastery in Saki, Poland
items.text_orig:
The Feast of the Transfiguration of the Lord was solemnly celebrated at the Monastery of St Demetrius of Thessaloniki in Saki, Poland, on August 18–19.

The celebrations began with an All-Night Vigil presided over by Bishop Warsanofiusz of Siemiatycze, with the participation of numerous clergy. At 11 p.m., an Akathist to St Demetrius, the patron saint of the monastery, was celebrated, followed by the first Divine Liturgy at midnight.

On the morning of the feast, the blessing of water was followed by a festal Divine Liturgy, again presided over by Bishop Warsanofiusz.

In his homily, Fr Rafał Wawreniuk reflected on the mystery of the Transfiguration and Christ’s revelation of His divine glory to Peter, James and John. He stressed that the experience prepared the disciples for Christ’s Passion and reminded them that suffering is not the end but leads to the Resurrection.

Following the concluding procession, Bishop Warsanofiusz emphasized that an encounter with Christ should lead to an inner transformation, strengthen faith and help believers face life’s difficulties with courage.

He encouraged the faithful not to limit spiritual experiences to passing moments, but to bring their fruits into everyday life through prayer, love for one’s neighbor and faithfulness to the Gospel.

The celebrations concluded with words of gratitude from Archimandrite Włodzimierz to the bishop, clergy and numerous faithful who had gathered for the feast.

Text: Fr Bogumił Korniluk, Photos: Łukasz Troc

items.title_orig: Light from the East: Masterpieces from the Ikonen-Museum Recklinghausen
items.text_orig:
Icon Museum and Study Center, Clinton, MA

October 16, 2026- March 21, 2027

Opening to the public, October 16, 2026, the Icon Museum and Study Center in Clinton, Massachusetts presents rare icons from Novgorod, Moscow, Crete, and Constantinople.

For the first time in the United States, highlights from one of Western Europe’s largest museum collections of Orthodox icons will be on view in the exhibition Light from the East: Masterpieces from the Ikonen-Museum Recklinghausen .

Gordon B. Lankton Gallery at the Icon Museum and Study Center Photo by John Cannon

Drawing on the riches of the Ikonen-Museum in Recklinghausen , Germany, Light from the East journeys back in time 500 years beginning at the dawn of the 20th century in the final days of Imperial Russia, through the splendor of Venetian Crete in the 16th century, to arrive at the austere beauty of medieval Novgorod and the final glories of Byzantium.

By the Russian Revolution of 1917, the icon had stood as an emblem of Russian political and religious identity for nearly a millennium, asserting continuity between Tsarist Russia and the Byzantine Roman Empire. When Byzantine capital Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Turks, Moscow asserted itself as the center of the Orthodox church and proclaimed its imperial status as the Third Rome and political successor to the Byzantine Empire. Moscow’s ambitions to unify Russia into a single state saw the distinct regional iconographic styles like that of Novgorod—which itself went back to the very origins of Russian icon painting in the 12th century — absorbed into Moscow’s unified imperial style.

After the Fall of Constantinople, Greek artists and scholars found patronage within the colonies of Roman Catholic Venice. On Crete iconographers blended the elegance of Renaissance art with the timeless spiritual authority of Byzantium and produced masterpieces prized by both Orthodox and Catholic clientele. Yet, when the Ottomans captured Crete in 1669, icon painting in the Eastern Mediterranean contracted again, taking on a regional approach as artists produced icons with more modest means for local markets.

By the fifteenth century, Greek and Slavic icon painting had grown into distinct branches on the tree of Orthodox iconography, at times intertwined by shared artists and Orthodox faith, at other times separated by wars, conquests, tastes, and trends. This exhibition testifies to Greek and Russian icon-painters grappling with the rise and fall of empires at the dawn of modernity.

The five icons presented here, offer a glimpse of this rare opportunity to examine 30 masterpieces of Russian and Greek iconography from Western Europe’s largest museum collection of old Orthodox Icons, presented in the contemplative galleries, and idyllic setting of the Icon Museum and Study Center, in Clinton, MA.

Annunciation at the Well Early 20th century Egg tempera on wood, basma with filigree and enamel Mstyora, Russia Loan 2026.01.04, 40 Photo credit Ikonen-Museum Recklinghausen

The End of an Age

Mary turns her head as she gathers water at the well, startled by a voice coming out of nowhere. Gabriel soars down from heaven calling out his greeting. Frightened, the young maiden runs inside and there receives the angel’s message.

This rare icon takes as its inspiration the account of Annunciation in the Gospel of James. The artist—a master Old Believer painter from the village of Mstyora—has suffused the image with a cool light, revealing a love for delicate pattern and texture in the rocks, leaves, and architecture that fill the scene.

When this delicate little icon was painted around the year 1900, it stood at one end of a tradition of Slavic icon painting that stretched back nearly 1,000 years. Despite centuries of political upheaval and military conquest that marked the years between 1453 and 1917 in the Orthodox East, icon painting persevered.

And yet, within a decade of this icon’s creation, icon-painting in Russia was banned under Soviet anti-religious law. The icon workshops that made up the economy of numerous communities throughout the Russian Empire were forced to close, secularize, move, or go under cover.

Saint Symeon the God-Bearer Late 16th century Egg tempera on wood Moscow, Russia Loan 2026.01.12, 443 Photo credit Ikonen-Museum Recklinghausen

Moscow

There is a bittersweet expression on the old man’s face. The righteous Elder Symeon, who had been told by the Holy Spirit that he would not die before beholding the Salvation of his people, now holds the Christ Child in his arms.

Despite the tenderness with which Symeon holds the baby Jesus, the child twists and turns as if trying to wriggle free. Icons and hymns of the Orthodox Church use this encounter between infant and elder as an opportunity to encourage the faithful to contemplate the mystery of Christ’s sacrifice. The child is shown squirming with fear and exposing his left leg, a common artistic shorthand for the bodily suffering he would undergo, while his face remains resolutely fixed on the elder who prophesized Christ’s willing, redemptive death. With eyebrows furrowed, Symeon looks past the child, off into the distance as he prepares to depart this life in peace.

The delicate lines of Symeon’s hair, the rich gold of the background and Christ’s robes, and subtle expressions on the faces are typical of the refined courtly style of icon painting that gained popularity in 16th and 17th century Moscow.

Saint Nicholas of Zaraysk with Scenes of his Life End of the 15th century Egg tempera on linden wood Novgorod, Russia Photo credit Ikonen-Museum Recklinghausen

Novgorod

Legend recalls that an icon like this one—showing Saint Nicholas standing with arms outstretched—was present at the baptism of Vladimir the Great in 988. This event traditionally marks the conversion of Rus’ to Christianity.

In 1225, Saint Nicholas is said to have spoken through the icon to a local priest instructing the man to take his wife and child, and venture north bringing the miracle-working image to aid Prince Theodore of Riazan in his struggle against the Mongol invasion. On campaign in 1237, the prince was captured and later died. Upon hearing of her husband’s death, and rather than facing capture at the hands of the Mongols, Princess Eupraxia threw herself from the highest tower in the palace, clutching her infant son to her chest.

It is said that the town where this happened was renamed Zaraysk, from “zarazit’sya” meaning “to fall to one’s death,” in memory of the tragedy. The family would eventually be reunited in death and buried beneath the icon which came to be known as Saint Nicholas of Zaraysk.

The vivid icon before you, typical of medieval Novgorod, is an especially early copy of an iconography that would become popular throughout the Slavic world.

The Man of Sorrows Attr. Andreas Ritzos End of the 15th century Egg tempera on wood Crete Loan 2026.01.23, 345 Photo credit Ikonen-Museum Recklinghausen Photo credit Jürgen Spiler for Ikonen-Museum Recklinghausen

Crete

Christ’s head tilts to the left while his dead torso remains upright in an image that hovers out of time and place. Blood and water continue to pour forth from his side even as his death appears calm as sleep.

Icons like this were first used in Byzantine monasteries in the twelfth century during the Holy Week services. When the Crusaders sacked Constantinople in 1204, they brought images like this one back to Western Europe with them. In Rome, a Byzantine mosaic of the Man of Sorrows became the focus of a pilgrimage that attracted thousands from as far away as England and Scandinavia and inspired generations of artists by this deeply moving subject matter.

This icon, attributed to master iconographer Andreas Ritzos (1421-1492), carefully follows the traditional Byzantine way of depicting the Man of Sorrows . Yet the presence of three nails on the crossbeam, as opposed to four nails depicted according to Orthodox tradition, suggests the iconography was adjusted to appeal to Roman Catholic clients. Ritzos, like other Greek icon painters, made devotional images for both Orthodox and Catholics.

Saint Luke Painting the Mother of God Hodegetria Early 15th century Egg tempera on wood Constantinople or Crete Loan 2026.01.14, 424 Photo credit Jürgen Spiler for Ikonen-Museum Recklinghausen

Byzantium

The evangelist pauses, his brush hovering just over the surface of the icon. Before placing the last dab of gold on the star over Mary’s shoulder, he looks up, past the easel, out of the frame of the icon to the subject he is painting.

Ancient church tradition holds that the Evangelist Luke painted the first icon—a portrait from life of the Virgin Mary and Christ Child. We do not directly see the subject of the icon on which Luke fixes his gaze. Instead, the Mother of God in the icon on the easel meets our searching eyes with an expression of calm assurance. With her hand she shows the way.

Painted around the year 1400 either in the imperial capital Constantinople or on the island of Crete, this icon is a masterpiece of late Byzantine iconography. It was once a part of a multi-panel icon, pieces of which are now held at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Marianna Latsi Collection in Athens, and the National Museum of Stockholm.

West Gallery Exterior at the Icon Museum and Study Center Photo by Anna Farwell

Light from the East: Masterpieces from the Ikonen-Museum Recklinghausen is held in celebration of the Icon Museum and Study Center’s 20th Anniversary. As an institution dedicated to sharing, preserving, and studying the riches of Eastern Christian Sacred Art, we welcome local and international visitors of all backgrounds to encounter the holy image in a contemplative setting situated in small-town New England.

The exhibition opens to the public on Oct. 16. A conference running from Oct. 15-16 will feature talks by historians of Orthodox iconography from Germany, Greece, Russia, and throughout the US and Canada. This event is open to scholars, students, and all members of the interested public.

For more information and to register, please visit iconmuseum.org/symposium-2026

items.title_orig: Warsaw Cathedral celebrates Feast of St. Mary Magdalene with Pan-Orthodox gathering
items.text_orig:
The Orthodox Church in Poland solemnly celebrated the feast of St. Mary Magdalene, Equal-to-the-Apostles, on August 4, with festive services at the Metropolitan Cathedral of St. Mary Magdalene in Warsaw, the principal church of the Polish Autocephalous Orthodox Church.

Clergy and faithful from dioceses across the country gathered for the cathedral’s patronal feast. The celebrations began on the eve of the feast with an All-Night Vigil led by Archbishop George of Wrocław and Szczecin, in the presence of Metropolitan Sawa of Warsaw and All Poland, together with other hierarchs and clergy.

On the feast day, two Divine Liturgies were celebrated, with the main service presided over by Metropolitan Sawa and concelebrated by Archbishop George, Archbishop Gregory of Białystok, Bishop Gerasim of the Orthodox Church in America, Bishop Paweł of Hajnówka, and numerous clergy.

In his homily, Archbishop George reflected on St. Mary Magdalene’s unwavering love for Christ, emphasizing that true gratitude to God arises from a personal encounter with His grace. He noted that the saint became one of the first witnesses of Christ’s Resurrection because her love overcame fear, reminding the faithful that the Risen Lord is recognized above all with the heart.

Addressing the congregation at the conclusion of the celebrations, Metropolitan Sawa described the Warsaw cathedral as the spiritual mother of all Orthodox churches in Poland, saying that its feast is a celebration for the entire Church. He encouraged the faithful to imitate St. Mary Magdalene’s steadfast faith, courage, and devotion to Christ, stressing that the commemoration of the saints is not only about honoring them but also about following their example.

During the festivities, the Order of St. Mary Magdalene was awarded to Matushka Maria Bogus in recognition of her many years of dedicated service to the Church. Archbishop George also received birthday wishes and was presented with a commemorative enkolpion by Metropolitan Sawa.

The celebrations concluded with the Metropolitan’s blessing and a festive reception in the metropolitan gardens. Due to ongoing restoration work at the cathedral, the traditional procession was not held, although pilgrims were able to view the progress of the renovation, including newly installed mosaics adorning the cathedral’s exterior.

Source: Orthodox Church of Poland
